questions.question: August Weismann, a German biologist, argued in the late 1800s that the cells which become eggs and sperm must pass through a 'reduction division' that halves their number of chromosomes. Each human body cell holds 46 chromosomes, and at fertilisation an egg and a sperm join into one cell. Why must the sex cells carry only half?
questions.answer: To keep the count from doubling every generation
choices: To keep the count from doubling every generation
To give the child an equal share from each parent
To weed out harmful genes before they pass on
To let the child keep the stronger copy of each gene
questions.context: If eggs and sperm kept all 46 chromosomes, a child's first cell would hold 92, and the count would double again in every generation; meiosis halves it to 23 in each sex cell, so the child starts with 46 again. Each parent would give an equal share with or without the halving, and the halving does not pick out the healthy copy of a gene or the dominant one. Edouard Van Beneden had already seen, in the eggs of a roundworm in 1883, two divisions that halve the number.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (NGSS HS-LS3-2, TEKS Bio 8) teaches meiosis as the division that halves the chromosome number for sex cells, and why the number must stay the same from one generation to the next.

questions.question: Each of a woman's 23 pairs of chromosomes holds one chromosome that came from her mother and one that came from her father. As meiosis makes her egg cells, the pairs line up across the middle of the cell, and each pair is parted, one chromosome to each side. Which of the chromosomes from her parents end up together in one egg cell?
questions.answer: A mix, each pair sorting by chance on its own
choices: A mix, each pair sorting by chance on its own
All 23 from her mother, or else all 23 from her father
The same 23 in every egg cell that she makes
From each pair, the one with more dominant genes
questions.context: Each pair faces either way at random, whatever the other pairs do, so an egg can get any mix of her mother's and her father's chromosomes: 2 multiplied by itself 23 times, over 8 million mixes, before crossing over adds more. This independent assortment is one reason no two of her eggs, and no two brothers or sisters other than identical twins, are quite alike. Which partner goes to which side has nothing to do with dominant genes.
questions.grade_note: Independent assortment of chromosomes in meiosis is the ninth-grade mechanism (NGSS HS-LS3-2) behind the variation that eighth grade states as a fact.

questions.question: Thomas Hunt Morgan and his students at Columbia University bred fruit flies by the thousand in milk bottles. The fly's genes for white eyes and for miniature wings both lie on its X chromosome, and in 1911 Morgan found that the two traits passed down together more often than chance would give. Yet some young flies got one trait without the other. How did Morgan explain those flies?
questions.answer: The paired chromosomes had swapped matching pieces
choices: The paired chromosomes had swapped matching pieces
A new mutation had changed one of the two genes
One of the two genes had moved to another chromosome
Stray flies from other bottles had got mixed in
questions.context: Morgan proposed crossing over: in meiosis the two partners of a pair lie side by side, break and trade matching stretches, so a gene for white eyes can end up on one chromosome with a gene for normal wings. Frans Janssens had described the X-shaped crossings, chiasmata, in 1909, and in 1931 Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock saw the swapped pieces under the microscope in maize. A mutation changes a gene, while crossing over only regroups genes already there, so the chromosomes passed on can be new patchworks of the two partners.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (NGSS HS-LS3-2) teaches crossing over in meiosis as a source of new gene combinations, and Morgan's linked fly traits are the classic evidence for it.

questions.question: Alfred Sturtevant, a student in Morgan's laboratory, put his homework aside one night in 1911 to draw the first map of genes on a chromosome. He took how often crossing over split two genes on the fly's X chromosome as a measure of how far apart they lie. Testing three genes at a time, he found that the percentage for one pair came out close to the sum of the percentages for the other two pairs. What did that show?
questions.answer: The genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place
choices: The genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place
The genes lie in a clump, with no fixed order
The genes shift place from one fly to the next
The genes are spaced evenly along the chromosome
questions.context: Only along a line does the distance between two genes equal the sum of their distances to a third gene lying between them; in a clump, or with genes that moved, the percentages would not add up, and adding fixes an order, not equal gaps. Genes far apart are split more often because more of the places where the partners may swap lie between them. His 1913 map placed five genes of the X in an order later confirmed, and one percent of crossing over is now called a centimorgan.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology connects crossing over to linked genes, and Sturtevant's map is the standard how-we-know case of reasoning from counts to a model.

questions.question: Gregor Mendel crossed a pea plant with round yellow seeds and one with wrinkled green seeds, and every seed of the first generation came out round and yellow; round and yellow are the dominant traits. He let those plants pollinate themselves and sorted 556 of the seeds they bore. About what share were round and green, a mix that neither of the first two plants had?
choices: About three in sixteen
About one in sixteen
About one in four
About nine in sixteen
questions.context: About three seeds in four are round and, on its own, about one in four is green, so about 3/4 x 1/4 = 3/16 are round and green; Mendel counted 108 of the 556. His full count, 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green, is close to 9:3:3:1, so nine in sixteen is the round yellow share, and the new mixes show that the genes for shape and colour sort into sex cells independently. Had the two traits travelled as a pair there would have been none, and genes lying close together on one chromosome come near that, giving only a few.
questions.grade_note: The dihybrid cross and its 9:3:3:1 ratio are named in ninth-grade standards (TEKS Bio 8B) as the test of independent assortment.

questions.question: A snapdragon that breeds true for red flowers, crossed with one that breeds true for white flowers, gives offspring with pink flowers. Neither allele of the colour gene masks the other, so a plant with one of each comes out in between. A grower crosses two of the pink plants and raises their seeds. How should the flowers of the new plants come out?
questions.answer: About one red to two pink to one white
choices: About one red to two pink to one white
All of them pink, like both of their parents
About three pink to one white
Half red and half white, with no pink
questions.context: Each pink parent passes on its red allele or its white allele by chance, so about one seedling in four gets two reds, two in four get one of each and come out pink, and one in four gets two whites. Red and white come back because the alleles never blended; only their effect in a plant with one of each is in between, a pattern called incomplete dominance. Carl Correns found the same pattern in the four o'clock flower in the early 1900s.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (TEKS Bio 8B) teaches incomplete dominance with red and white snapdragons giving pink.

questions.question: Karl Landsteiner, working in Vienna, mixed the serum, the liquid part of the blood, of himself and his colleagues with one another's red cells in 1900 and 1901. Some mixes clumped, and he sorted people into groups A, B and C, later renamed O. His students Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli then tested 155 people and found four whose red cells were clumped by group A serum and by group B serum alike. What did those red cells carry?
questions.answer: Both the A marker and the B marker
choices: Both the A marker and the B marker
Neither the A marker nor the B marker
One marker halfway between A and B
A third marker, unlike both A and B
questions.context: Group A serum attacks the B marker and group B serum attacks the A marker, so cells clumped by both carry both, and the group was named AB; it is group O cells that carry neither and are clumped by neither serum. An AB person carries an A allele and a B allele, and each makes its own marker in full, a pattern called codominance, unlike the pink snapdragon's in-between colour. By showing which donors suit which patients, Landsteiner ended the lottery of transfusion, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1930.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (TEKS Bio 8B) teaches codominance through AB blood, and Landsteiner's clumping test is the discovery behind the blood groups.

questions.question: Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern showed in 1910 that the A, B and O blood groups are inherited, and they then proposed two genes, each carried in two copies: one for A or no A, and one for B or no B. Felix Bernstein, a German mathematician, argued in 1924 for a single gene with three alleles, A, B and O, of which each person carries two. Which finding in families could tell the two ideas apart?
questions.answer: Whether an AB parent ever has a group O child
choices: Whether an AB parent ever has a group O child
Whether two group O parents ever have a group A child
Whether two group A parents ever have a group O child
Whether an A parent and a B parent have an AB child
questions.context: Under the two-gene idea an AB parent who carries a no-A copy and a no-B copy can pass on both together, so an O child is possible; Bernstein's AB parent has only an A allele and a B allele to give, so every child gets one or the other. The other three findings fit both ideas equally well. Counts of the groups in whole populations, and the families studied after, bore Bernstein out, apart from very rare exceptions found much later, and the ABO gene is now known to lie on chromosome 9.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (TEKS Bio 8B) teaches multiple alleles through the A, B and O blood-group alleles, and asking which result would decide between two models is ninth-grade reasoning about evidence.

questions.question: John Dalton, the chemist, described his own colour blindness in 1794, and since his brother shared it, he judged that it ran in families. Red-green colour blindness of this kind affects about 1 man in 12 of Northern European descent, but only about 1 woman in 200. Why is it so much rarer in women?
questions.answer: A woman needs the faulty gene on both of her X chromosomes
choices: A woman needs the faulty gene on both of her X chromosomes
A man passes the faulty gene on only to his sons
The faulty gene is dominant in men but recessive in women
Women have their colour vision tested far less often
questions.context: The genes for the eye's red-sensing and green-sensing pigments lie on the X chromosome. A man has one X, so a single faulty copy shows; a woman has two, and one working copy is usually enough, so she is colour-blind only if both carry the fault, and a man passes his X to his daughters, never to his sons. A study of Dalton's preserved eye in the 1990s found that he lacked the gene for the green-sensing pigment.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (TEKS Bio 8B) names red-green colour blindness as a sex-linked trait more common in males.

questions.question: Queen Victoria never showed signs of haemophilia, an inherited illness in which the blood fails to clot properly, and no case is known in her family before her. Yet her son Leopold had it, and two of her daughters, Alice and Beatrice, who never showed it either, had sons who did. What best explains that pattern?
questions.answer: Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes
choices: Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes
Victoria carried the faulty gene on both of her X chromosomes
Her husband, Prince Albert, carried the faulty gene and passed it on
The faulty gene arose new in Leopold, by chance
questions.context: A carrier passes her faulty X to about half her children: a son who gets it has the illness, and a daughter who gets it becomes a carrier in turn, as Alice and Beatrice did. Two faulty copies would have made Victoria ill herself; a father gives his sons his Y, so Albert could not have given it to Leopold; and a change arising new in Leopold could not reach his sisters' sons. Through her daughters it reached the royal families of Russia and Spain; a genetic study of the Romanov remains in 2009 showed it was haemophilia B, and it most likely began as a new mutation in Victoria or her father, though no one can be sure.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology (TEKS Bio 8B) names haemophilia as a sex-linked trait, and Queen Victoria's family tree is the standard pedigree for it.

91991a730c.why: Judge (medium): the lure 'To keep the child from copying just one parent' was dead (both sex cells join, so no one reads the halving as stopping a copy of one parent). Replaced with 'To let the child keep the stronger copy of each gene', the real dominance mix-up (that a sex cell keeps the dominant copy; F35: a sex cell gets either allele, half the time each). The setup no longer spells out the sum ('holds the chromosomes of both the egg and the sperm' is now 'at fertilisation an egg and a sperm join into one cell'), as the judge suggested; still told at the level of cells. Context now says the halving picks out neither the healthy nor the dominant copy, without saying 'by chance' (the independent-assortment key).

54f9469ff3.why: Fact-check (uncertain) and judge (low): 'no two brothers or sisters' overreached, since identical twins come from one egg and share their chromosomes. Context now says 'other than identical twins' (F33). Stem and choices unchanged.

783e854af3.why: Fact-check note (optional, taken): 'giving every egg and sperm chromosomes that are new patchworks' is not true of the fruit fly in this question, whose males do not cross over. The last clause now says only that the chromosomes passed on can be new patchworks. Stem, choices and key unchanged.

cecb405a9b.why: Fact-check (error): the 1913 map placed five genes, not six; two of the paper's six 'factors' (C and O, white and eosin) never recombined and sat at one place, and proved to be forms of one gene (F31). Context now says 'five genes'. Judge (low): 'rate' could be read as a speed, so the stem now says 'percentage' for the share of young in which crossing over split a pair.

453bf5b797.why: Fact-check (error): genes lying close together on one chromosome give only a few new mixes, not none; the context now says so (F32). Judge (low): 'None of them at all' sat oddly under 'About what share' and was the only choice not starting 'About'; replaced with 'About nine in sixteen', the round yellow share, for a player who half-remembers 9:3:3:1. Stem and key unchanged.

7749057df6.why: Fact-check (uncertain): Correns's four o'clock paper appeared in December 1902 (Grokipedia says 1903), so the context now says 'in the early 1900s' (F34). Stem and choices unchanged.

492df4a3fb.why: Judge (low, taken): the stem said each person carries two copies under Bernstein's model but not under the two-gene model, which hid the step the key turns on. The two-gene model is now 'two genes, each carried in two copies' (F24: 'two independent pairs of genes'), and the context says plainly how an AB parent could pass on no A and no B. Choices and key unchanged.

6b4b4caa63.why: Judge (medium): 'What does that pattern show about Victoria?' ruled out by its grammar the two lures that are not about her (Albert; a new mutation in Leopold). The stem now ends 'What best explains that pattern?', and the choices are the judge's: two about Victoria (one X, both X's), Prince Albert as the source, and a new change in Leopold. The key's fact is unchanged (F26, F30); the context now says why each rival fails.
